newsitem.title: USA: Vitamin A derivative may offer cancer hope.
newsitem.headline: Vitamin A derivative may offer cancer hope.

text.p: U.S. scientists said on Tuesday they had found strong evidence that a synthetic version of vitamin A can fight cancer by making tumor cells self-destruct, opening a new and less painful route to cancer therapy.
The chemical is a retinoid known as 4HPR, and experiments have shown it can cause cancer cells to commit "suicide", they wrote in a report in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute.
Reuben Lotan and colleagues at the University of Texas in Houston said a buildup of free oxygen radicals somehow seemed to restore the natural self-destruct process.
Most cells usually die automatically when they are damaged or just too old. But in cancer this process, known as apoptosis, fails.
The result is uncontrolled cell growth and a tumor.
Various studies have shown that retinoids can destroy cancer cells including leukoplakia, a type of tongue cancer, and cancers of the head, neck, lung and liver.
Retinoids have also been tried against cervical cancer in a combination with interferon, a natural immune system substance.

Lotan said 4HPR might trigger apoptosis by causing a toxic build-up of free oxygen radicals inside cells that had already turned cancerous. Free radicals are charged molecules that react easily with other molecules and are believed to help cause cancer by damaging cell DNA.
Lotan's group grew cervical cancer cells in dishes and exposed them to 4HPR. The more of the compound they put on the cells, the more cells died off.
They looked at the dead cells and found fragmentation of the DNA characteristic of apoptosis.
Italian researchers told a recent conference in Houston that they had tried giving 4HPR pills to women with breast cancer and seen some positive results.
"We clearly see effects of the 4HPR on cell viability and we see that it can induce apoptosis," Lotan said.
"It is a promising agent but the clinical trials that are now ongoing will have the final word. If it kills cancer cells then obviously it can be used in cancer treatment."
Ethan Dmitrovsky of the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in New York said 4HPR might prove useful in combination therapy.
"Such treatment may benefit patients who already have cancer or prevent cancers from arising in 'high-risk' individuals," he wrote in a commentary on the report.
